parts.title: 🪑 Assigned Desks Are Quietly Returning to Some Offices
parts.part1:
After the pandemic, hot-desking became more common. In this system, workers are not given one personal desk. They choose an empty desk when they arrive.

Now, in some offices, the desk map is changing again. Assigned desks are returning, and some workplaces are reducing their reliance on hot-desking.

It raises a simple question: after years of sharing, why are some workplaces choosing personal desks again?
parts.part2:
A worker may once again have a regular place to sit each day. But this is not a full return across the office world. Some offices still use shared desks and flexible office space.

The result is a mixed picture. The personal desk is back in some places, while the shared desk remains part of the wider office model.
parts.point_one_heading: Why a personal desk feels different
parts.point_one_body:
Workers’ daily experience may be part of the story. Korn Ferry points to complaints about hot-desking: less appeal than working from home, unwanted closeness to unfamiliar colleagues, and less predictable workspaces.

In Gensler data, assigned-seat workers reported belonging more often than workers without assigned seating: 87%, compared with 74%. They also reported effective focus more often: 80%, compared with 67%. These are associations, not proof that desks caused the difference. Against this background, some offices are bringing assigned desks back.
parts.point_two_heading: A limited return, not a market reversal
parts.point_two_body:
The wider market tells a different story. In CBRE’s 2024 survey, the share of companies with at least one desk per employee fell from 56% in 2023 to 40% in 2024.

Respondents expected it to fall to about one-third by 2026. So assigned desks are returning in some places, but shared seating remains part of the wider office model.
parts.in_one_line: Assigned desks are making a quiet comeback, but the shared office has not disappeared.

parts.title: 🪑 The Desk Is Back—but Not Everywhere
parts.part1:
For some office workers, the race for a desk may be ending.

After the pandemic, many offices began using hot-desking. In this system, workers do not have their own desks. They use an empty desk when they arrive.
parts.part2:
Now, some companies are changing this plan. Scotiabank and iCapital Network are among the companies bringing back assigned desks in some parts of their offices.

The change is quiet. It is also limited. Not every office is returning to one desk for every worker.

So the office is facing a simple question:

Should a desk belong to one person, or to whoever arrives first?
parts.point_one_heading: A desk can feel like a place to belong
parts.point_one_body: Gensler data shows why the change may matter. Among workers with assigned desks, 87% said they felt they belonged at work, compared with 74% without assigned desks. Also, 80% said they could focus well, compared with 67% in hot-desking settings. Korn Ferry says changing desks and nearby coworkers can make work less predictable. These findings help explain the return in some offices.
parts.point_two_heading: A small change, not a full reversal
parts.point_two_body: But the desk story is not moving in only one direction. CBRE found that companies with one desk or less for each worker fell from 56% in 2023 to 40% in 2024. In the same survey, 42% of organizations had more than 10% of their office space in flexible areas, up from 36%. Assigned desks are returning in some places, but flexible workspaces remain common overall.
parts.in_one_line: The personal desk is coming back for some workers, but the shared office is still here. For now, companies are choosing different desk plans for different workplaces.
